newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Worrisome wheat fungus found in Tennessee.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Worrisome wheat fungus found in Tennessee.

text.p: The karnal bunt fungus, which roiled U.S. wheat marketing earlier this year, was discovered in Tennessee, officials said Thursday but they foresaw little impact this time on exports.
"It's very, very isolated and a tiny amount of wheat," said a senior advisor to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. "It should not have any appreciable effect at all."

Many nations refuse to accept wheat that contains the fungus. The Agriculture Department persuaded grain customers to continue to buy U.S. grain by issuing documents to prove the wheat did not come from an infected area.
As one of the world's largest wheat exporters, the U.S. sells billions of dollars of wheat to foreign buyers each year.
"We will continue to provide additional declarations to countries that the wheat they are accepting is coming from regions where karnal bunt is not known to occur," Drazek said.
Karnal bunt imparts a unpleasant, although harmless, odor and taste to wheat flour. It also reduces yields and wheat quality.

At the close of trading, wheat futures prices at the Chicago Board of Trade were unchanged to 9-3/4 cents per bushel lower because of the karnal bunt discovery and on word the European Union was boosting its wheat export subsidies.

Tennessee officials said extraordinary measures would be taken to control the spread of the fungus. The steps, which would be taken in conjunction with the Agriculture Department, could include disposal of contaminated wheat, sanitizing grain bins and setting up a monitoring program.
Control efforts also can include compensation to farmers and millers.

A grain sample taken from a farm bin in Giles County, Tennessee, tested positive for the fungus, state officials said. Samples from seven other counties -- Coffee, DeKalb, Greene, Hamblen, Marion, Overton and Warren -- were believed to be positive.
So far, the fungus has been found in small areas of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, California, Alabama and Tennessee. The regions produce a small portion of U.S. wheat.
Drazek said the campaign against karnal bunt would ultimately be successful despite the new discovery.
"It's not at all surprising that we would find some spores outside the original quarantine area," he said. "Our feeling now is the quarantine is still operative and will be successful."
Jim Bair of the Millers National Federation said the latest discovery would have no impact on the milling industry unless the Agriculture Department began to quarantine or regulate wheat movements.

Earlier this year, the department agreed to offset the cost to millers for heat-treating a wheat byproduct as a step to assure the fungus did not spread. Otherwise, millers said, they could not afford to handle the wheat.
